criterion_notes.c1: Examines residential household water consumption from Dhaka Water Supply & Sewerage Authority (DWASA) across formal settlements, slums, and nine DWASA zones in Dhaka city.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (plain=no, narrow=no). Under the plain wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this is an econometric residential water demand study whose primary exposure of interest is household per capita monthly income (estimating income elasticities of water consumption), alongside demographic, wealth-proxy, monthly bill expenditure, settlement-type (formal vs. slum), and geographic DWASA zone controls; it does not empirically examine a governance, institutional, legal, or regulatory factor. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no rule-type mechanism governing service access is analysed as an exposure: (1) all metered households faced a single uniform DWASA tariff rate (11.02 BDT per 1,000 L, used algebraically to impute water volume from the bill paid), and increasing block tariffs (IBT) and smart metering are merely proposed as policy recommendations in the conclusion rather than empirically evaluated; (2) the 'fixed pay' dummy (unmetered households paying a fixed charge) has a bivariate correlation reported in Table 2 but is explicitly assumed by the authors to have no direct causal path to water consumption and is used solely as an excluded first-stage instrument for endogenous household income; and (3) formal-vs.-slum location and DWASA zone dummies are treated purely as socio-economic/spatial controls without examining tenure rules, eligibility criteria, documentation, or administrative regulations.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative study analysing 2018 cross-sectional survey data from 459 households in Dhaka collected by BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD) using OLS, 2SLS instrumental variable regression (IVREG), and instrumental variable quantile regression (IVQREG).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports per capita per month household water consumption (quantity in litres, imputed from household monthly water bill divided by the uniform DWASA tariff rate and household size), including distributional differences across consumption quantiles, formal vs. slum settlements, and spatial zones.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (459 residential households in Dhaka city, expressed per capita per month), primary exposure (per capita monthly household income instrumented by fixed-pay status, plus socio-economic and spatial covariates), outcome (log per capita monthly water consumption in litres), and study design (cross-sectional econometric survey analysis using OLS, IVREG, and IVQREG).

evidence_quotes.quote: Using 459 household survey data collected by BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD), this study estimates income elasticities of water consumption after controlling the effects of other covariates including wealth-proxies, location, household size, water bill and spatial zones using the instrumental variable regression (IVREG)

Water consumption data was collected in 2018 from 459 households located in nine different water zones of the DWASA. The dependent variable used in this study is the per capita per month water consumption.

This study uses fixed pay dummy as an instrumental variable, which has the property that changes in payment mode are associated with changes in income but do not lead to changes in water consumption in the current settings of Dhaka city.

Household water consumption is calculated based on water bill paid by the households. The water bill paid by households has been divided by the DWASA tariff rate effective since 1st July 2018 at 11.02 BDT (USD 0.13) per 1000 L, to calculate the total water usage of the households per month.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 19 of 21 (Section 5 Summary and Conclusions)
evidence_quotes.quote: Therefore, introducing increasing tariff blocks (IBT) as water consumption might promote water conservation, ensure more access to water by households belonging to the poor blocks and generate more revenue for the DWASA. However, DWASA must ensure smart water meter to the residents before implementing such tariff structure.

raw_response.exposure: Per capita monthly household income (instrumented using a fixed-pay unmetered billing dummy), with controls for household savings, formal vs. slum settlement location, household size, appliance/fixture wealth proxies (shower, washing machine, geyser, high commode), monthly water bill expenditure (BDT), and DWASA spatial zones
raw_response.outcome: Per capita per month household water consumption in litres (imputed from monthly household DWASA water bill net of 15% VAT divided by the uniform tariff of 11.02 BDT per 1,000 L and household size)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 459 residential households in Dhaka city (77% in formal settlements and 23% in slums) across nine DWASA water zones, surveyed in 2018 by BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD); unit of analysis: household (measured per capita per month)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper empirically examines residential household water consumption (quantity) across 459 households in Dhaka city using 2018 survey data and OLS/IVREG/IVQREG methods (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its exposure of interest is household per capita income (estimating income elasticities of water demand) alongside demographic, wealth-proxy, and spatial covariates. It does not examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing service access under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2: all metered consumption is imputed from a single uniform DWASA tariff rate, fixed-pay unmetered billing is explicitly modelled as having no direct effect on water consumption and used solely as an excluded instrument for income, formal-vs.-slum and DWASA zone dummies serve purely as socio-economic/spatial controls without analysis of tenure or eligibility rules, and increasing block tariffs (IBT) are only discussed as a concluding policy recommendation.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional household survey analysed using ordinary least squares (OLS), two-stage least squares instrumental variable regression (IVREG), and instrumental variable quantile regression (IVQREG)
